title: Australia's ID verification crackdown and the US crypto reporting U-turn
summary: Australian banks are tightening ID checks under AML/CTF Act reforms, sparking a public debate. Meanwhile the US Treasury kills its unhosted-wallet reporting rule. Two stories, two very different signals about where the global AML perimeter is heading.
script:
ALEX: The United States Treasury has just scrapped a rule that would have required financial institutions to report crypto transfers of more than ten thousand dollars to unhosted wallets, and I want to lead with that today because my read is that it sends a signal far beyond American borders. Jordan, is this a story for Asia-Pacific compliance professionals or is it noise?

JORDAN: It's absolutely a story for this audience, but I'd push back on your framing slightly. The way you're telling it, listeners might walk away thinking the regulatory tide is going out on crypto. I don't think that's right at all. What I think this is, is a jurisdiction-specific tactical retreat on one instrument, not a change in the underlying direction.

ALEX: Fair. Walk me through why you read it that way.

JORDAN: Because the pressure on virtual asset service providers in Singapore, in Hong Kong, and in Australia has not slowed down. MAS is still tightening its licensing framework. AUSTRAC is still expecting tranche-two entities, which now include lawyers, accountants, and real estate agents, to stand up compliant programs. The United States pulling one proposed rule does not change any of that. What it does do is remove a useful benchmark that some compliance teams were already quietly using as a floor for their own unhosted-wallet monitoring thresholds.

ALEX: That's the interesting operational point. Because when a major jurisdiction proposes a rule, practitioners in other jurisdictions often use the draft standard as a reference even before it's enacted. So what happens now to that informal benchmark?

JORDAN: It disappears, which is a problem. If you're an MLRO at a licensed digital asset exchange in Singapore or at a crypto custody operation in Hong Kong, and you had built your transaction-monitoring thresholds partly by reference to where the United States was heading, you now need to justify those thresholds on their own terms. That means going back to your risk assessment, anchoring the rationale in the MAS digital payment token service requirements or the HKMA's virtual asset guidance, and making sure the logic holds without leaning on a now-withdrawn foreign proposal.

ALEX: And the read-across to the Anchorage Digital and Standard Chartered partnership that also landed this week is relevant here. Anchorage is a federally chartered digital asset bank regulated by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. Standard Chartered, which is a regulated entity in Hong Kong, Singapore, and Australia among other jurisdictions, is now offering USD-denominated accounts and Swift wire access to eligible non-US institutions through that partnership. So the infrastructure for crypto-to-traditional finance connectivity is expanding even as the United States is retreating on one reporting rule.

JORDAN: Which is exactly why I'd tell any MLRO who read the headline about the US withdrawal and felt relieved to stop and think again. The rails are getting broader. The correspondent banking relationships are deepening. Your counterparty risk exposure to digital asset entities is probably growing this quarter, not shrinking.

ALEX: Let's move to Australia, because there's a genuinely interesting tension playing out there. The AML/CTF Act amendments are driving banks to intensify identity verification requirements for existing customers, not just new ones. And that has triggered a public debate, with the Australian Banking Association's CEO speaking to ABC Brisbane about it this week. Jordan, I want to get your practitioner read. Is this a compliance story or a customer experience story?

JORDAN: It's both, and I think that's what makes it uncomfortable for compliance teams right now. You've got existing customers, people who have held accounts for years, suddenly being asked to re-verify identity. And the public reaction is suspicion, not cooperation. People are asking whether it's a scam. Which is, by the way, a completely rational question given the impersonation scam environment we're operating in across the region right now.

ALEX: So you've got a compliance obligation that is triggering the exact behaviour pattern that fraud teams are trying to counter.

JORDAN: Exactly. Banks asking existing customers to submit identity documents creates a channel that scammers will attempt to clone. If I'm the head of financial crime at an Australian authorised deposit-taking institution right now, I am making sure my fraud team and my AML team are in the same room designing the re-verification outreach. Not separately.

ALEX: I'd add a supervisory angle here. AUSTRAC's scrutiny of customer identification programs under section 84 of the AML/CTF Act is real and ongoing. The annual board-level review of the AML/CTF program is a live obligation right now for many Australian institutions. The customer identification component, which is Part B of the program, is precisely what's under pressure when you extend verification obligations to existing customers. Boards need to see that Part B has been updated to reflect the amended Act, not just the original obligations.

JORDAN: And if your board review has already been signed off this cycle without that update, that's worth flagging to your group compliance head before the next audit cycle opens. Don't wait for AUSTRAC to ask.

ALEX: Before we close, two obligations worth flagging for listeners. If you're at an HKMA-supervised authorized institution and you received a deficiency letter from the HKMA's thematic review of suspicious transaction report narrative quality, that closure process is overdue. About a quarter of the authorized institution population received those letters earlier this year. If yours is still open, that needs to be on your risk committee agenda this week, not next.

JORDAN: And for Singapore-based compliance officers, the quarterly STR governance review under MAS Notice 626 is a standing obligation. That means reviewing completeness, timeliness, escalation effectiveness, and reconciling STRO acknowledgements. If your last review was light on documentation, now is the time to tighten it before year-end audit pressure arrives.

ALEX: The through-line today is actually about perimeter uncertainty. The US pulling back on unhosted-wallet reporting, Australia expanding its identity obligations to existing customers, and crypto infrastructure connecting to traditional banking rails through partnerships like Anchorage and Standard Chartered. These are all different expressions of the same underlying question, which is where exactly does the AML perimeter sit now.

JORDAN: And regulators in this region are not waiting for the United States to answer that question. The full obligation register and source links for everything we discussed today are at amlagents dot streamlit dot app. Before end of week, if you're in Australia, check that your Part B customer identification program reflects the amended Act. If you're in Hong Kong, close those thematic review findings. Those are the two calls to make.

ALEX: We'll be back tomorrow. Watch for any further AUSTRAC guidance on the tranche-two implementation timeline. That is the next shoe to drop for non-bank compliance professionals in Australia.
